I so wanted to like this game, but simply cannot. 

UX that seems designed specifically to annoy and infuriate players - illogical, too many clicks / button presses to achieve anything, and NPC conversation lock-in that requires an specific exit step to make it go away... the developers must truly hate the players to release such pain on us.

A general clunkiness and lack of polish that makes vanilla Skyrim feel smooth and modern also doesn't help, and neither does quest design that totally fails to capture the attention or imagination. The faux "Old English" is a terrible idea that loses any of its initial "cuteness" by the time the second NPC interaction is done, and the voice acting is so terrible I find myself reaching for the mute button to make the NPCs shut up.

Also, 3 save files only - REALLY?!?

Add to all the above a slew of frequent early game crashes (I haven't yet made it out of the early game due to a proliferation of bugs, black screens, and crashes to desktop - with or completely without mods), and this is a game that totally and utterly fails to make me even almost like it.

Pity... but, yukk.

Exploration is fun, graphics and sound are crisp. Gameplay and progression is satisfying. Story is average but the writing is pretty good in these constraints. 
If you enjoy Skyrim, Crimson Desert and the like, get this game.

I have finished the game, and my god, the story is bad. You should not come here expecting a decent, let alone good, story. That said, the gameplay is where it shines. The game offers a good selection of classes, called vocations, each with its own skill set and combat rhythm. Every vocation plays differently, and mastering those differences feels satisfying. The world is absolutely gorgeous and thoughtfully designed. Enemy placement makes exploration and traversal engaging.

The game is all about spectacle above narrative depth. And those spectacles made a great emergent narrative a lot of times.

Dragon's Dogma 2 is an excellent successor to the first game. Managing to expand and enhance the scale and scope of the original in almost all areas! The sense of adventure and exploration in this game is, in my opinion, vastly superior to any of it's contemporary competition.

It's greatest strength lies in its dynamic world and the encounters within them. Every journey across the open world is different from the last because of the variety of ways different events play out. You could find a journey via Ox cart ambushed by an Ogre in the middle of the night, throwing off your planned journey and forcing you to improvise. Or you could be kidnapped by a Griffin and taken off course entirely. This keeps the game feeling interesting even after dozens of hours and you can still be surprised over 100 hours in!

The game also rewards creativity in combat encounters and exploration. There are a variety of ways you can use your abilities or interactions with pawns to traverse the map or fight enemies. If you have a crazy idea to take down an enemy or reach a difficult spot, try it and you might be surprised! There are also hidden caves and woodland paths leading to obscure areas all over the map and you will still find new things to discover on a second playthrough.

This is where I feel the game's most controversial feature is its greatest strength. The limited fast travel. Upon launch this was met with scorn, as if Capcom didn't understand game design, and the ability to teleport anywhere at anytime is now just a given in modern games. The journeying from place to place is a core part of this game's experience and what makes it fun. Removing that takes away all the fun and defeats the point entirely. It seems some people no longer want to PLAY games and just wish to complete an interactive checklist as efficiently as possible before rushing off to the next shiny new thing. The inclusion of the Eternal Ferrystone should satisfy these people to to some degree as it allows unrestricted fast travel at anytime so long as you travel to a place first to put down a Portcrystal, opening up a nice middle ground.  

The game's most unique feature which deserves much more recognition than it gets, is the pawn system itself. The character customisation available here is some of the best I've ever seen and can really result in some amazingly creative pawn encounters in the world. Once a pawn is created, you are able to assign them to a number of different vocations and customise their equipment to make the perfect companion that is right for you. This companion can then be hired out by other players to join them in their adventures and can return with gifts as well as knowledge from their time away. Thid can be useful, such as knowing the location of new chests and dungeons, or the weak spots of enemies you have yet to encounter! The system allows you to create a 4 person team that compliments your play style perfectly and can be tweaked and changed to meet your needs or make up for any weaknesses in your chosen vocation. 

The only criticisms I have of the game come down to its vocation system which, while deeper in some ways than the first game, is more limited in choice. With popular locations like the Mystic Knight and Assassin missing, along with their associated skills. However each vocation the game does have feels more developed than in the first game. The abilities are more dynamic and open up  a varity of different playstyles within them that you can tailor to your liking. The game also lacks secondary weapons for classes like the Archer and Magic Archer. Which were present in the first game. However, recent changes increasing the number of abilities equippable at any one time, goes a long way to rectifying this and increase the depth and creativity offered. One thing that would improve this drastically would be to remove the rearmament skill from the Warfarer. It is clunky and wastes a skill slot. It would be a much more fun to play if using the associated weapon skill would automatically allow you to switch weapons, without the need for a dedicated skill to do so.

The knock down feature also feels incredibly excessive sometimes. If you're unlucky you'll find yourself slipping and tripping across terrain or being knocked about like a ragdoll and unable to move. Though this can be mitigated by equipment and augments.

The game did launch with significant performance issues on PC which unfortunately left a bad first impression that the game struggled to recover from. It is now in a much more stable place after several performance patches and runs far better then something like Monster Hunter Wilds. Which seems to have been given much more grace for it's long term performance issues for some reason.

I hope that the upcoming Dark Arisen expansion will only improve on an already incredible game and bring in new players, alongside its release on Switch. I whole heartedly recommend the game to anyone who thinks they might enjoy it as there has never been a better time to try it!

Bought it when it was on sale while knowing what the complaints were on release. But I thought that a game this expansive with a DLC coming and a rumored huge patch early September might be worth it for the reduced price. 

Now, having lost myself 90 hours deep in the blink of an eye playing this game I can confidently say that my money was more than well spent. 

The good: 
- The performance. This game is amazingly optimized (now) and I don't think there is another game quite this big that runs so smoothly on my very mid PC. People recently have been parrotting "what removing denuvo does for your game", but this level of optimization runs much deeper than just removing that malware. There is genuine effort deep into the core logistics of how this game renders expansive environments and cities cluttered with NPCs
- The pawn combat AI is surprisingly apt (and at times also the total opposite) and it makes for a enticing moments where I just watch in awe how they handle fights
- This game has surprising depth. What I mean is that there can be combat (and sometimes also quest solutions that might seem a little outlandish, but do in fact work. Medusa Head might be the greatest fun I had with a game mechanic I had in a while
- The detailed character customization options for player and main pawn. Just creating my wet dream of a partner down to the shape of their double chin was already quite funny alluring, but then seeing the creations of other players like literal loot goblins kept the game fresh in a very fun yet immersion breaking way. I miss you, little fat loot goblin
- The world is rich with secret spots and hidden items. There is always a sense to explore a crevice or ravine. I will say tho that this gets undercut by the first point of the bad I will mention below. Despite the bad I still enjoyed finding something even if it wasn't all that rewarding or "hidden" after being led there
- You can highfive your pawns on command

The bad: 
- This game's story is extremely, almost offensively holding your hand hard. This is also true for hidden chests or caves. Luckily, they don't outright give you the solution to every single problem, but still ... Pawns from other players will have already seen every secret and lead you there directly instead of just indicating a direction. It almost felt insulting to one's intelligence. Still, I found myself using their services at least a handful of times when I was in the mood to doze off
- There is a good variety of side quests that at least to me didn't feel overwhelming in number. And yet when they didn't outright hold your hand to the solution the tips to solve the quests/solutions were so obscure or obvious that the fun of doing the quest wasn't all there. The memorable side quests stick out a bit more, because most of the quests are quite bland and undemanding OR frustratingly and badly explained by the NPCs/logbook. This was too much of a black/white situation for me
- I previously praised pawn AI, but now I also have to dunk on it. They seem more capable at complex and obscure interactions than something like collecting items that are directly in front of them/me. Or they specifically leave that area to me, because we are a team and such. But I wanna be lazy and let them do all the carrying
- The pawns are quite prone to running into zones that spell certain death for them
- Pawns can interact with you directly to lift you high up, but there is no command or combination of commands to actively trigger them. You can point to items that are high above you, but the items need to be visible from your POV which they aren't in like 95% of cases. There definitely needs to be combination to force pawns (outside of combat) to lift you like "Help + Go"
- Some weapon/armor upgrades (and not always the final upgrade) require a material that is only available during the end end end game and said end game is also not permanently available once you reach it. Awful design, but quickly remedied by just shuffling around data
- While there is a lot of unique armor sets to be collected, most of them look or feel very same-y. There is like maybe 1-2 out of 10 sets per vocation that are distinct from the rest. I would have wished for DD2 to be just a tad bit more bold when it comes to aesthetic variety

Conclusion:
Highly recommend. This game undersells itself. The pricing feels like theft, but you are stealing from CAPCOM, because you get so much out of this. The bad may seem like it outweighs the good, but I wouldn't have lost myself for almost 4 days of total time if the bad was really that BAD. The bad just makes my eyes roll, but the good makes me want to play just 1 more hour ... until it's suddenly morning.

[h1]The game is a colossal waste of potential.[/h1]
It could have been easily 10/10 game, but it's basically worse in every aspect, than it's predecessor, except for combat. DD2 is not finished, but biggest problem is that it was made for Goyjins in mind - who hates fun, likes to slowly walk and when the game plays for itself, instead of Nihonjins. At least new DLC should be the step into the right direction and recent patches are proving it.

Combat is the strongest part of the game and improvement over the first one, where it was already good. Ability to walk on big monsters really feels great. 

Player Movement is not responsive for the sake of "realism" and often character does unintentional movements (unlike DD1). The camera is also too close to the players back and you can't change the distance or FOV.

Sadly, there is now only 1 weapon per Vocation (except for Warfarer), which is very anti-fun decision. It is also a step back in terms of Vocations - no more Long Bow and Mystic Knight. Soldier, Warrior, Magic Archer, Magician and Sorcerer. Are simmiliar to the first game with some QoL changes and as enjoyable as they were before. Archer skills... it has less skills than the first game, but most annoying part of them are elemental arrows - they require Skill Slot AND Consumable Arrow. While aiming with bow Mouse Accelration is applied which can't be turned off. Thief has Double Jump, but as a separate skill. One of its master skills is just a complete joke - auto-dodge incoming attacks for very low stamina cost. Is there a person (besides netorare fans) who likes when the game plays itself? Trickster is just perfect for them. It has some (2) fun skills, which will make other enemies fighting each other or manipualte them to make them fall from the clif. But, why those aren't just skills for Magician? Making a whole class which basically DOESN'T DEAL DAMAGE in a ACTION game? Mystic Spearhead is the only new vocation, but it rather disappointing and could have been better. Warfarer - class which allows you to use all other classes weapons and majority of skills. Needs skill swap mod to be fun.

Open World is stayed on the same level for the most part. There is total of 2 zones - European planes and hills with forests and desert valley. There is also Volcanic Island, which is just 2 X-like corridors - empty, nothing to look at besides Hot-Springs. Clearly unfinished.
All those areas share the same problems:
 - Exploration is barelly rewardable, because 95% of chests are filled with stuff like "3 rotten fish" or Gear which can be easily bought from shops. Another important change - the chests aren't respawning, so that worsless reward is not random and no point in revisitng the area. 
- All areas are tightly packed with the same type of enemes (goblins, bandits, lizardmen, harpies) and their recolored variations, which are differing only by 1-2 attacks and elemental resistances. 
- Traversal - lack of Portcrystals and limited Ferrystones forced normal players to waste time on walking and waiting for carts. I'm glad that with previous update the game went away from that garbage design and added more Portcrystals and Eternal Ferrystone.

Dungeons are a pathetic joke. 1st game had not many dungeons, but each of them was pretty big, unique and filled with different types of enemies. This game has around 70 caves, which look absolutely identical and have like 2-3 corridors, and only 1 actual mediocre dungeon.

Enemy Variety is also disappointing. The game has 3 new boss type of enemies:
- Medusa, which has only 1 (one) spawn in the open world.
- Dullahan, has probably 2 or 3 spawns, but his moveset is rather poor.
- Worm, which only appears once or twice in the Post-Game.
Can't call Minotaurs a new type tbh. In case of normal enemies - Slime is the only true new addition. Repaints also disappointed me - what is the difference between Green Goblin and Normal Goblin? Green one is ambushes you and that's it. If there is more - I didn't notice. Others are just using different type of damage and have different elemental weakness. There is also no more different type of Drakes - only classic which is combo of 3 different drakes from the first game and another drake is absically an "undead" version with weak points. Lastely, it doesn't have Hydra, Cockatrice or Evil Eye from the first game, so it is basically 1 step forward and 1 step back.

Story breakes multiple canons of the first game and unfinished. Characters aren't interesting or memorable at all, without any uniqness (besides being black or furry). Battle vs dragon is a downgrade in comparison to DD1 - comes suddenly and it's just one couple of minutes fight. Post-Game is hidden for unknown reason, because you need to be a viewer of video essays to not to discover it, because the game points out towards it almost as it uses the yellow paint. [spoiler] It also doesn't matter who will be your lover - no unique scenes or sex, like it was in the first game. Character with the biggest affinity will just appear in the hand of the Dragon for a 3 seconds and thats it.[/spoiler] 

Quests for the most part are just ok. They are just there to fill the quota. For 1 exception and it's ofcourse Sphinx's riddles, which is sadly spoilered by everyone and you most likely already know / knew the answer to at least some of the riddles.

Post Game is a kick in the balls for any DD1 fan. Making it time-limitted, where you have 10-12 in game days (sleeps) to get everything done until the game is over. Furthermore:
- The new bosses do not respawn. 
- All gear from the Unmoored World chests can be bought from shop.
- The game doesn't tell about the point of no return and if you complete it - the game will delete the saves from Unmoored World so you need to complete it again get into Unmoored World again just to spend there SOME time. 
No unique dungeon like Everfall from the first game or any fun to have at all. But, at least video-essayists could make a "content" about "2" appearing in the title of the game...

Performance after the recent update noticably increased, but the current state is just "playable". I'm getting 40 FPS (native 1080p). Game should perform much better with the picture it renders (for a graphics which are looking worse than one game from 1967 which I hate a lot). People who says that performance is good while playing with DLSS should get higher standards. Performance still decreases in Inventory and Skills menus.

Character Creator - disappointment. It's actualy hard to make a beautiful woman. You really need to spend some time to make a character NOT to look ugly. The hairstyles are also limitted. If you don't believe me - use "Random" option and check how many of them end up not ugly. The minimum height is only 150cm (we all know why). Variety of voices is also very poor.

DD2 also lost many details - Greatsword attacks can no longer harvest Ore. Ogres no longer become excited after seeing a woman and doesn't get Poison after eating a man, etc. There is SOME stuff, like ability to fly on Griffin, or to use mirror-shield against Medusa, but its not much. It aslo filled with REALLY ugly NPC. There is too many blacks in my european part of the map. Elfs (the race with a really long lifespan and beautiful appearance) - half of the village are ugly or elders. There is also just too many furries. I wish there was no furries, but just blacks who are habbitans off Desert area, instead of first area. At least it would make sense.

The things I also wanted to pay attention to - Capcom was selling unfinished game for 70$ and didn't fix it for 2 years. The release version didn't have New Game button. But do you know what button did it have? Online Store. DLC had higher priority than a New Game button.

Concluding, it's hard to recommend the game even after multiple patches, because the whole game needs to be remade to be good.

This game is hard to recommend. Dragon's Dogma 1 was magic. It was jank, and lacking in so many ways, but it had such a charm.

[h2]TLDR: Final thoughts[/h2]
I think most people would agree that DD1 is the better game, because at the very least, it feels like a fantasy adventure. It has a vibe that is very hard to describe and while it does have the same problems, DD2 has made them worse not better.

Having said that all that, I recommend it, barely, (like 51% yes, 49% no). I think it's worth experiencing. The core gameplay is fun and addictive, but there will be many moments where you just go "Why?!". 
The performance after the September 2026 patch is also Amazing. It's the reason I finally bought the game.

Give it a shot, I'm sure you will find something that scratches an itch that often isn't found in other games, but don't expect a masterpiece. At best expect a cult classic like DD1.

[h2]Combat[/h2]
It's great. It's heavier and slower, and the new Vocations are genuinely interesting and fun. I won't spoil the mystery vocations so you can discover for yourself. But imagine fantasy Darth Maul and find it ASAP. It was a blast. 

Pawns are an issue. They often don't use their skills designed to open new strategies to the arisen or other pawns. This was common in DD1 and you could really use it to help define a play style or strategy. It's missing here for some reason.

Enemy variety is also lacking. DD1 had this problem to but Jesus the first 20 hours were all Ogres, Cyclops, harpies, goblins, and Saurians.....so many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Saurians. This was another opportunity to improve upon the first game, and somehow it feels worse, although I could be misremembering. DD1 was also lacking even at the beginning of the game.
Gameplay on normal difficulty feels way too easy. I barely had to try until I found a dragon for the first time and even then it didn't feel hard just that the dragon had a ton of health. I would recommend a harder difficulty at the start so the core gameplay systems actually feel more impactful.

Overall the combat is the highlight even if it feels like a downgrade sometimes. Which vocation you play is going to change the experience a lot, and there is reason to try all of them. Augments can be used between vocations and can round out your play style. Though it may mean playing a vocation you don't have fun with (Archer is boring AF personally). 

Stats will re-balance when you change vocations so there is no fear of leveling the wrong stats, by staying in 1 vocation too long. You can min-max still like in DD1, but it's like a 5% difference. in DD1 you could actually brick a character If you stayed fighter or some other Vocation too long and switch to a Sorc/opposite stat Vocation later in the game, your stats would be mostly stuck as physical or magical depending on the class you poured the most levels into, making you a ♥♥♥♥ Magic character. But in DD2 have no fear. Switch to your hearts content.

[h2] 
The Story so far
[/h2]
The story also is lacking. You had years to think of a story and characters to flesh out the world and themes, and pretty much did the same thing as DD1. There are no stakes. No actual central conflict that gives you a reason to care. I get that this is a re-imagining of the first game, but damn can we have some actual plot and character development. Side stories? The conflict between Vermund and Battahl is not even set dressing. It's barely a focus, and pretty much only serves as a reason why people are racist against the Cat People, and even that idea is not fleshed out. It's also an idea that has been done to death.

The first game's story wasn't great, but at least it established a clear conflict and motive from the very beginning. Hell the opening hours of DD1 are honestly magical. The rest of the  game doesn't hit those same heights, but it's still a charming solid game.

My main gripe is that they had the opportunity to really make a world. Not just one for the eyes but one for the mind. One that resonates with your heart. And they just didn't. Fancy graphics and good combat seems to be where 90% of development went.

Even just adding more dialogue to pawns to flesh out lore and the world would have been a great decision. The pawns are millennia old. They have seen so much between different universes. Why do they just repeat the same old trite ♥♥♥♥ again and again?

[h2]Pawns[/h2]
Pawns somehow are worse than DD1. Pawns were always a cool and great idea, but somehow their dialogue and usefulness is more limited here than in DD1. They have fewer dialogue lines and repeat constantly. Pawns aren't as interactive in combat as the trailers led us to believe. They often don't open up collaborative gameplay opportunities even when they have the skills equipped to do so (the fighter springboard skill being an obvious example. They just never use this mid combat, even when the enemy is 200 ft tall.) Dragons Dogma 1 the pawns used skills like these way more often to open up new strategies.

and again, - Why didn't they use pawns as an opportunity to add flavor/lore into the world?

[h2]Why buy it?[/h2]
DD2 feels less cohesive than DD1 somehow. They are both games with disparate ideas that don't ever come together, but it's worse here. The one thing this game does capture, and often times even more than DD1 is exploration. The core gameplay idea in DD1 and DD2, is that you have to face the scary unknown.

You need to prepare; you need to learn. Though the game is really easy at first. Might be worth starting on a harder difficulty. You need to get comfortable with exploring the unknown day or night. Often times the game rewards you taking the longer more unknown/difficult route. And this combined with the combat is the best part.

You explore the unknown, engage in fun combat, make small discoveries, and sometimes have incredible combat encounters (like when I accidentally rode a griffin across the entire map when fighting one for the first time. Terrifying and cool AF). It just sucks that after so long all these really cool ideas barely or didn't grow in execution and they are still disconnected from each other.

So Ok I have spent 70 hours now and will spend more in the future. I like too much of this game to just forget it, so here is some tough love.
I will only focus on the downsides of the game because, here starts the copium, because I believe in Dragon's Dogma 3 to be a GOTY. This is not.
Here is my list of issues:

-the engine is 1:1 the one from the first title. This feels overall like a 1.5 rather than  2 title. Yes I know, according to the lore yada yada, NO.

- the character tries to climb all the edges that it shouldn't and fails to grab the one it should, especially when jumping or using levitate. also, it seems that at times the character doesn't go in the desired direction, even if the camera has moved, especially after climbing, being knocked down or subject to other incapacitating statused.

-pawns randomly do not recognize ladders, get stuck against objects like lamps because they try to move in a pack and there is not enough space. Often they linger far so when there is an abrupt fight they be chilling back

- sliding is way too easy on inclined (89 degrees instead of 90+ degrees, I don't mean to do some mountain goat climbing) surfaces and it almost feels like the character is bouncing off the terrain with an accelerating factor on the movement vector. the game actively behaves in different ways on a climbable surface that has a sharp or round edge, in the latter case the player will fail climbing and be sent sliding off the path, possibly all the way down a hill/climb to its death. this happens because even if there are large ledges available, because the sliding creates an acceleration vector that has the character taking several steps to regain the balance and often these steps are enough to go off the ledge.

- seeker's token on narrow surfaces are hard to grab because if the character stands exactly on it they cannot be grabbed, if the area is narrow the character would more easily fall than move to a position where the token can be grabbed -> these require better placement.

- finder's token, Sphinx parent antics -> can we have a game where playing the game is enough and 95% of the players don't have to look the solution on the internet? It is not 1990 where there is one game to engage with for MONTHS to find ONE THING. Do an ARG game otherwise. 

- the statues overlooking the view are implemented terribly, 10/10 times I have already explored the place. Basically reaching the statues is waaay off the path and more of a deliberate choice, instead reaching the places they point at, comes naturally with exploring.

- increase monster variety if you do a map this big, reskins with different behaviours are fine, but the map here is way too big compared to the variety, reskins included.

- do something more with the lore? DD2 is pointing in a good direction, don't dwell on it and don't chase dark souls.

- remove the damn cinematic for Portcrystals when the player is TWO STEPS AWAY, the time it takes me to get there is the time you make me waste in a useless cinematic pointing at an object next to me that already stands out from the backdrop. Otherwise make the cinematic start from when the character enters the town.

- "!" on the map are horrible, they point at a generic area without height indication, most of the times it is a damn rolling rock. I know I can push them, I don't care, they are 99% times useless. Do a better job with visual effects to make an important item visible (seeker token easy to see at night is fine). 

- I know why oxcarts are in the game, but remove ferrystones and just give fast travel by default. Travelling by foot to collect seekers token or find equipment is enough time padding, I cannot imagine the horror of moving around before the 2026 patches.

- Quests are found too randomly (e.g. ghost oxcart, saint of the slums...), or like by being at a certain point at a certain time, when the moon is in the house of Sirius or something. Also engage in some variety and indications, interpreting the goal of a quest is sometimes the only engagement with the quest itself.

- slightly related, the warrior/sorcerer quest line was implemented well, but finding the hybrid vocations was quite the meme, by following the main quest they are found so late into the game, what if I don't want to do a 2nd playthorugh? Then it is just a matter of doing a short conversation for vocation and meister skill, it looks like someone dropped the ball. Just pick a lane and stick to it, the current state makes it feel like the hybrid vocations where just slapped into the game at the last moment.

- on the same topic, the hybrid vocations offer risible benefits, one would never trade mettle for, dunno, moving faster when carrying objects?! even restoring stamina when defeating an enemy is not worthy because enemies rarely come in waves and smaller groups are dispatched quickly. At this point why not making these small QoL "augments" something that is just unlocked for the character and not requiring an augment slot? Otherwise re-design the hybrid vocations, right now they are just an afterthought.

- the warfarer exists for utility (levelling all vocations, even the ones players do not like -> they don't mean to engage with anyway) and for fun (fashion choices), why gate behind so much randomness? (same randomness issue as the point above).

- more pawn lines (have them have a tracker for stuff like materials and illness, they repeat the same tutorial lines over and over), possibly dedicated vocations, and rework dragonsplague or the new similar mechanic, it is genuinely game breaking in some event combinations. 

- jeez hire another couple VAs, I heard the same guy (very good VA btw, nothing to complain about his efforts!!) for 70% of the game, spread across random NPCs and more or less important characters.

The 1.0 of this game was a genuine insult to the face of the fans. 

Oh btw, open world a-la-ubislop are done, just don't. Big maps = unique content, or do not bother. Like you even removed epic quest arcs like the Griffin chase from the original DD, it seems you do not know what to do with a giant map other than copy pasting random same-y camps, caves and monsters.

[h1]---PATCH 3.2 SHOULD HAVE BEEN THE LAUNCH STATE---[/h1]

This is my first review post of DD2 and actually finished the game for the first time since release. To put it into context I couldn't stomach the game and never completed it after 60+ hours on a first play through due to the jank, technical engine issues, stuttering (on the same exact PC last year) as well as just awful systems set in place out of arbitrary reasons that made it a far inferior product than it's cult-hit predecessor. 

Patch 3.2 changed that and it should have been the launch state of the game, with key takeaway right out of the bat is the much improved technical / performance optimisation, M&KB improvements as well as the 6 skill and fast travel amongst other in-game system QoL additions. After patch 3.2 I could not get enough of the game and hope Dark Arisen expansion will deliver more than expected. Definitely worth on a sale considering it's improvements for a single player RPG experience unlike other competitors in the gaming landscape.

[h3] PROS  [/h3]
+ Unmatched combat feedback / Vocation system; I just wish there are more like DDON
+ Pretty Graphics, Capcom's inhouse engine looks great and have the low fantasy aesthetics if you like the grounded design over high fantasy; nothing like it in the current market. If you use DLSS5 the game will hold up visually for the next decade.
+ Unique pawn / party system with their much improved AI and 6 slots, pawns are a force to be reckoned with.

[h3] CONS  [/h3]
- Story might as well be non-existent, it's there but doesn't even compare to the themes of the first game.
- Capcom should consider making Dragon's Dogma into a co-op lite game considering all the foundations are there, we already had DDON so any lore reasons is pointless argument.
- you can definitely feel the game had development hell issues and production, as well as rushed feeling to the story and late stage of the campaign. Hopefully Dark Arisen for DD2 will provide the dungeoneering-loop experience close to the idea of BitterBlack Isle from the first game+expansion.

The gameplay is very enjoyable. One of the complaints i see was the lack of variety with the monsters but imo it isn't so lacking that you fight the same enemies over and over, but after a certain point you definitely feel it. But the main highlight is definitely its' combat. The combat is a mix of Monster Hunter and Final Fantasy XV and is definitely very inspired by those games to a certain degree. The weapons and skills are very satisfying to hit and the variety of classes make it so that if you get bored of one, you can switch to another, and they have transferable passive skills so its not all to waste. The highlights are definitely the fights with larger monsters. I love climbing on the back of a giant werewolf, stabbing it multiple times before it grabs me and hurls me 50 ft away (and off a cliff if im unlucky).

The world feels very much alive. Your companions always share their thoughts and suggestions in an unannoying way (and you can mute their voices if you're really irked by it, but honestly why would you) and the roaming npcs all have lives and schedules that they tend to. There are a couple of times where I'll be exploring the world and stumble into a house where a group of npcs are having an argument. Another time I'll be listening to a beggar telling a story about a monster, and all of a sudden a random minotaur attacks the city and the npcs all react accordingly.

The weakest part is definitely the story, where it is generally considered weak and flat. The story gets the crimson desert treatment where the game heavily focuses more on its sandbox gameplay than delivering a deep narative experience. So the story is whatever, personally the gameplay makes it worth it for me.

So overall i would definitely recommend Dragon's Dogma 2 to players new to the franchise/haven't played the previous games. To players who have played the previous game, it can definitely feel like you're playing the exact same game but with better graphics so if you like that then go for it. All in all i would give it a 7 to 7.5/10, above average, but nothing super innovative or too awe striking.

I finally bought Dogma 2.... character creation somehow has more options than Dogma 1, yet is entirely lacking in multiple options the first game had. Hair colors were made more realistic... but then we have green, stark white, crimson... yet not a single high saturation orange. Muscles are entirely lacking too. At best it's lines drawn on the character, as opposed to a physical model change like the first game.

But, that's all one thing. Then I got to Pawn Inclinations..... There are 4, and they all suck in various ways to the point where there are no good options. I'm a mage and want a tank pawn to draw aggro and protect me. My best options are Calm which pulls my pawn next to me, and the enemies alongside them, or Straightforward which has the pawn running headlong into combat. Technically that last one is fine, except the Pawn's voices are Inclination specific. So again, there are 4 feminine and 4 masculine.

In the first game I could have my pawn sound however I liked, and then also have them target larger enemies first, while also being ready to run to me if I need help. Such a thing is not possible anymore. You can't mix and match inclinations...

I think worst out of everything are the changes to the way the game controls. My character moves like a semitruck hauling molasses. There is no urgency in the sprint, yet it takes the same stamina. There is no snappy responsive movement. You have to slowly accelerate for everything, and it sucks.

Need to jump out of the way of a goblin flying at you? Hope you weren't already in the middle of an animation because it takes a full second to stop whatever you were doing, you can't cancel out of any skills you're casting, and then it takes another full second to accelerate so that you have the momentum to actually go anywhere with your jump. Sometimes that's okay, but here it's not because the flying goblin has already tackled you and is kicking you on the ground faster than you were even able to return to idle, let alone begin accelerating to jump out of the way.

That acceleration is mandatory too. If you just move the control stick and press jump, you go vertically. You MUST build momentum if you want to go anywhere.

And then mage combat, my beloved... You used to hold the staff out in front of you and have character recoil when you fired. Just a little bit. Now you don't even hold the staff up. You just have it awkwardly held at stomach height and the bolts fly out of it without recoil. No animation. Nothing.

Dogma 1 is a rough game. This is fact. Dogma 2 though.... Dogma 2 is somehow worse. It looks really pretty, sure, but that doesn't make up for what I consider to be a massive step backwards in terms of gameplay. Nothing replaces gameplay and the feeling it gives you. Nothing. If it feels bad, it's bad. To me, it feels bad. As such, for me, the game is bad.

I'm going to go start a new Dogma 1 save. Maybe I'll try Dogma 2 again a couple years from now. Hopefully the sluggishness will have improved by then.

Ich finde Dragon's Dogma 2 genial. Das Spiel schafft es für mich tatsächlich, genau den besonderen Flair des ersten Teils wieder einzufangen – nur in einer deutlich schöneren und lebendigeren Welt.

Gerade die Welt gefällt mir unglaublich gut. Sie wirkt wesentlich belebter als im ersten Teil, überall passiert etwas und die Welt fühlt sich dadurch viel mehr nach einem echten Abenteuer an. Gleichzeitig hat man trotzdem dieses typische Dragon's-Dogma-Gefühl behalten, das für mich einen großen Teil des Charmes der Reihe ausmacht.

Besonders begeistert mich das Pawn-System. Dass man seine eigenen Vasallen erstellen, mit ihnen durch die Welt ziehen und sie anschließend mit anderen Spielern teilen kann, macht mir richtig viel Spaß. Gerade weil ich Dragon's Dogma 1 damals nur offline spielen konnte, ist das für mich eine wirklich schöne Erweiterung des Konzepts. Man bekommt dadurch ein kleines Gefühl von Multiplayer, obwohl das Spiel selbst weiterhin ein Singleplayer-Erlebnis bleibt.

Was die Schwierigkeit angeht, empfinde ich das Spiel bisher allerdings als eher einfach. Vielleicht ändert sich das im weiteren Verlauf noch, aber momentan wünsche ich mir teilweise etwas mehr Herausforderung. Gerade deshalb bin ich gespannt, wie sich ein möglicher New-Game-Plus-Durchlauf anfühlen wird.

Technisch bin ich diesmal ebenfalls sehr zufrieden. Das Spiel läuft bei mir inzwischen vollkommen problemlos – keine Ruckler, keine Abstürze und keine nennenswerten Bugs. Besonders schön ist das für mich, weil ich Dragon's Dogma 2 direkt nach Release leider überhaupt nicht vernünftig spielen konnte. Dass sich das mittlerweile offenbar deutlich verbessert hat, freut mich umso mehr.

Ich werde das Spiel auf jeden Fall durchspielen und mir anschließend auch die Erweiterung gönnen.

Unterm Strich: Für mich fühlt sich Dragon's Dogma 2 genau wie das Spiel an, das ich mir als Nachfolger gewünscht habe. Es nimmt die Seele des ersten Teils, steckt sie in eine wesentlich größere und schönere Welt und gibt dem Ganzen durch das Pawn-System noch eine zusätzliche soziale Komponente.

Für mich bisher ein richtig starkes Abenteuer.

If you like DD1, you will like this game. If you LOVE DD1, as I do, you will not like this game. It pales in comparison to its predecessor in almost every way, while still being a solid Action-Adventure RPG in its own right. The combat is stellar, but less flexible than DD1. The armor and weapon system is great, but less complex than DD1. The graphics and story are better than the previous game, but that is a low bar to overcome. The pawn AI has improved and has more actions and map memories that the pawn can learn, and is one of the few areas I can say is a true improvement from the first installment.

The class system is a side step from DD1, and the lack of permanent character attached stat points makes additional playthroughs superfluous and removes the joy of min-maxxing characters from DD1. The enemy variety is also slightly improved, but at higher character levels there is nothing to challenge the player like albino hydras or the three species of high drake. The endgame area having a time limit was a terrible decision for gameplay, as you have to rush to try and collect everything or experience regular endgame monster fights.

As far as performance, I personally never experienced any issues, even on launch. The new patches have apparently fixed these, as well as a few minor issues with merchants, items and quests. Overall, I have mixed feelings about DD2 and walk away from playing this game feeling mostly frustrated at how it falls short from what it was previously. Here's to hoping for Dark Arisen II...

I've been holding out on this one since release and only occasionally glancing at it. This is a lot like the first one, if youve played that you know what you are in for. What really gets me here and why I recommend it so much is that it is probably the coolest adventuring world I've seen in a long time. The last game that made me feel this way was Elden Ring. Even though fast travel is an option, I don't want to do it, the world is that fun to explore. There is stuff everywhere, in every house, in every nook and cranny. The cave systems, the elaborate winding vertical cliffs, under waterfalls, it's all awesome. And with a decent system performance is really good now and the graphics constantly make me stop and just admire the beauty of the world they made. One of the best immersive adventuring games ever.

The survival elements are present even if a little light, with very dark nights and at times it feels borderline sim with really detailed physics. One time I had made it up to the top of a winding spire-like tower and took a moment to take in the breathtaking view. Then a harpy divebombed me and the physics of the hit pushed me forward just enough where I slow-tipped off the ledge to my death in a comedic tumble. I couldn't even be mad, the way it happened was more impressive than frustrating. Even walking on rough terrain will see you potentially tumbling off a cliff if you aren't careful. But these elements are done perfectly. Not overly so and not undercooked, just enough to make you feel invested in what you are doing at all times.

The pawn system is really refreshing. Combat is dynamic and classes actually matter a lot with pawns fulfilling a role for your party. There is way more to it than that but there is too much, you have to just play with the systems. Every class is significantly different with mechanics that change entirely how you play. Leveling vocations is actually fun due to this and the game encourages you to swap them and experiment.

There is tons to do in this game with so many intricate systems and most are intuitive. The character creator is probably the best I've ever seen, too. I wouldn't say the stpry is bad, it's just basic. This feels like a foreign world where your character doesnt have a voice and I like that, it is more immersive in some ways. The side quests are where it is at here because while they aren't that impressive themselves, the world is just so dang cool I find myself just exploring for the sake of it and they give you something to latch onto. it is actually the journey that is fun, the focus here is adventuring, exploring, and combat. Its one of those games you can easily get lost in without a concern for an intricate story. The structure is also very open and you can do things that in any other game wouldn't be possible, such as grab and hold onto a beast for a scenic view and hope you don't run out of stamina holding on for dear life.

Just a couple critiques - The game can be a bit easy but a hard mode is coming with the DA expansion. It is possible to abuse the pawn system for easy money, or recruiting one that is insanely strong. Id suggest not doing that and playing blind. This is a game where you can easily botch a quest if you aren't careful and fail it permanently. I do think that was a good design decision, I am glad to see a game that actually has a cost relationship with the player. You may think there are not many quests but actually there are quite a few and many are very easily missed. If you are someone that skips text thinking its just trivial banter, you should think twice in this game. You can also lock yourself out of quests if you progress the main quest too far. The game does imply this in dialogue, thankfully, so pay attention. another thing that I am finding is that I can just buy the best gear. I love that there is tons of gear and the designs are really cool but I also wish there was more unique stuff out in the wild. Gear is very expensive though so there is usually something to chase.

Absolutely a game worth paying $50 for. The work Capcom did with this one is stellar, it's really really good and I think severely underrated. It falls short in the narrative execution and I'd love to see them invest more in pawn/character interaction, and facial animations. also, Id love a 4 player adventure just like this. There are some areas of opportunity but nothing that makes me irritated. You can kind of tell they didn't have the budget they wanted and had to prioritize certain things. Between Philosophical Pretensions and Massive Technical Failures:

Here are my very first impressions of Dragon’s Dogma 2, and let’s not sugarcoat it: this game is an absolute trainwreck. I usually trust my gut when it comes to video games, and my initial impact with this title wasn't just problematic—it was infuriating. The experience stumbles before it even begins. The technical infrastructure tied to the RE Engine and the implementation of DirectX 12 are a complete disaster. Having to deal with amateurish bugs like the inability to launch the game in fullscreen, alongside frequent graphical glitches, immediately gives the impression of a completely half-assed, unoptimized product. Main menu navigation is clunky, and the core mechanics feel counterintuitive right from the start, even for versatile and experienced players.The introductory section offers a remarkably lackluster tutorial on basic combat and managing classes and "Pawns." However, while this whole framework might be crystal clear to anyone who played the first installment (which, in hindsight, feels almost like a low-budget beta for this sequel), newcomers will find themselves completely lost. There is a total lack of any proper guidance. The underlying narrative seems decent, but there’s absolutely no reason to expect a spectacular, innovative plot or characters you’ll actually care about. It’s interesting on paper, sure, but in reality, it's far from mind-blowing.The structural issues get significantly worse when you look at the user interface and navigation. The world map is an absolute piece of garbage. It is visually unreadable, utterly useless for actual navigation, and seems intentionally designed to disorient you rather than help. This total failure in layout mirrors a completely broken quest system where objectives are handed out randomly and carelessly, with zero respect for the player's time. You are given vague, half-baked instructions that lead to endless, aimless backtracking.This is where we enter the territory of the game's incomprehensible, pseudo-philosophical nonsense. No one expects to be held by the hand, but the game is so deliberately obtuse with its goals that the developers' choice to "sell" these flaws as a way to sharpen the player's wits makes me laugh. It sounds like the cheap rhetoric of a corporate personal-growth seminar, used as a pathetic excuse to mask blatant shortcomings in game design. The reality is that you often end up completing these poorly thought-out missions by sheer luck—and luck is just luck, it's not problem-solving.The idea that every single choice carries permanent consequences for the story is an interesting concept, much like the decision to include only one save slot. While this latter choice is terribly frustrating and punishing, I admit it successfully gives real weight to your actions. The real issue is how poorly it's executed. The game auto-saves very rarely and only to the default slot; resting in populated areas creates a checkpoint you can reload from, but the risk of losing hours of gameplay due to a single misstep or oversight is sky-high. This draconian limitation is a massive flaw that, for now, leaves me with a highly cautious and far-from-positive assessment.The combat system is another sore point, completely orphaned of a targeting system worthy of the name. There are fights where the camera and the controls make you feel like a total klutz—a drunkard flailing aimlessly in the air—even though a tremendous amount of work clearly went into making the physical weight and reactions of combat realistic.Ultimately, for the time being, I find Dragon’s Dogma 2 to be an extremely slow, frustrating, and at times, downright boring game. Having spent so few hours with it so far, I can't help but wonder how long it will take before I get permanently sick of it. As of today, I highly doubt I'll have the patience to ever reach the endgame. I reserve the right to change my mind down the road, but for now, this formula hasn't won me over at all. It's a pretentious mess disguised as a masterpiece.

I waited eleven years for this game, as someone who played the original Dragon's Dogma when it came out. For eleven years I knew what to expect from Itsuno's work and yet when I originally played Dragon's Dogma 2 when it came out back when I played on Xbox I had a... discouraging time with it. After several updates, and a few years passing I acquired my PC and figured "hardly anyone plays on Xbox anymore and my pawn isn't rented at all. I should get it on PC and maybe even try out some of the mods folk made." This was prior to yesterday's and the previous update, so I came to Vermund to find it in a better place performance wise, but it was still plagued with those nitpicks I had. And thankfully in my case, mods were able to plug those issues.

Issues that were then almost entirely fixed with these new patches in preparation for Dark Arisen.

The game's performance is no longer terrible, and I can get 60fps while playing on high (.25). There is a cure to dragonplague so now if folk want to cure their pawns without issue they can do that, but now there are benefits to actually having your pawns be plagued. The new corrupted monsters have given us a taste with how difficult Dark Arisen is going to be (and it's honestly on par with the difficulty tweaks I had done with difficulty mods) and to know there's a Hard Mode coming with the expansion too has me excited to truly get lost in the endless repeating gameplay of Dark Arisen, the thing that was frankly missing from the base game. We had the exploration and sense of wonder from the base game. It's now time for the system to keep players coming back for more to be added.

I still have some small issues with the story, but after spending the last couple of years actually thinking about the story and looking over every single little detail in the story it all ends with an oddly satisfying conclusion. One that anyone who paid plenty of attention to the story and mythology of Dragon's Dogma and Dragon's Dogma Online would find satisfying. To the average player who is more interested in the gameplay it would sound like rubbish, but as Itsuno himself once said "everything in this game is intentional."
There's a lot of details for anyone to find, details to clue the player into the happenings of your origin and the things that just come out of nowhere.

Short Review:
Hail, Arisen! It's good and only getting better! One of my favorite adventuring games out there.

Long Review:

I've been a fan of the series since its beginnings, and though this game had its flaws and performance issues, I've been thoroughly captivated by its world. You and your main pawn (a companion NPC) adventure across the land, exploring and taking on quests. You can hire two additional pawns, either Capcom-made or pulled from other players, to round out your party. Safety in numbers, Arisen! Pawns are genuinely a pretty unique and cool system in this game.

The launch was a troubled one, but a lot of the performance issues have since been addressed, and they've added more settings to help tune things for your system. Even on more robust rigs, cities like Vernworth and Bakbattahl can still see some frame drops, but for me at least, the latest patch has smoothed things out considerably.

On content: Enemy diversity is a little lacking, though it didn't bother me too much — I'm hoping the upcoming expansion helps fill that out. The main story feels a bit light in places (I suspect some things were cut or rushed, though that's just speculation on my part), but it's solid overall. Side quests are more of a mixed bag — some are genuinely great, others forgettable. I do feel parts of the story could've been deeper and more explored; it feels like a bit of a missed opportunity. My guess is the expansion will run its own separate story, so hopefully that either fleshes out the original or brings something interesting in its own right.

On atmosphere and difficulty: The atmosphere is fantastic, it genuinely feels like you're trekking on an adventure and camping out along the way. That said, difficulty does taper off significantly at higher levels, most content becomes fairly trivial outside of corrupted enemies (added in the latest patch) or Unmoored World encounters. From what's been shown of the expansion so far, it sounds like it's aiming to address exactly this for higher-level Arisen and their pawns.

Bottom Line: Get lost in a world worth adventuring through. See the sights, roleplay a little, and enjoy the ride. It can be a genuinely great time, flaws and all.

[h3]A Masterpiece with Mixed Reviews[/h3]

Even though people have mixed feelings about this game, I think some of them are simply misunderstanding what this game is trying to achieve. So, I'll give you a few reasons to dive into this wonderful adventure.

First of all, there's the combat, and that's something almost everybody agrees on: it's one of the best combat systems we've seen so far.

There are diverse classes (Vocations), each with a unique set of skills, and every class feels completely different. Because of that, choosing a class isn't just about picking the one that deals the most damage. It's about defeating your foes in different ways, or even leveling up different Vocations to unlock useful passive abilities for your favorite ones.

The second thing that makes this game unique is the world. It's a medieval fantasy world that may remind you of Skyrim, but at its core, it's a VERY Japanese game that has a lot in common with Zelda. It's an open world built around exploration, with chests around every corner that make you want to open them or figure out how to reach them, countless caves to explore, enemies to defeat, and quests to complete.

It's a top-notch open world that's not too big, but somehow feels immense. It's packed with big and little adventures around every corner, and sometimes a seemingly small discovery can lead you to something much bigger.

And then there's the story and the quests. Some people say the story is bad and that the characters are flat and not very deep. I partially agree. Some quests could definitely be more interesting, and I wish there were more cutscenes, especially because the quality of the cutscenes is superb.

But I don't think the game is trying to tell a story in the traditional way. It's more about the experience and how the world makes you feel. There are often different ways to achieve your goals, and oftentimes DD2 doesn't tell you exactly where to go or how to do something. Instead, you're given a general objective and left to figure out the rest yourself.

The game also doesn't constantly throw huge cutscenes at you to tell you what is happening. This makes the world feel more believable: you're not always being led down a predetermined path. Instead, you're creating your own story.

Just an ordinary elf asking for a bow. At first glance, it seems like an insignificant little task. But could it lead to something more?

And as for the characters, I agree that some of them can feel kind of flat, and the amount of time you spend with them can be surprisingly short. But in the end, it can all start to make sense. The story may seem just okay at first, but by the end, you might realize that there is something much more metaphysical going on underneath it all.

And even though some quests or interactions may feel clumsy, DD2 is insanely well-crafted. The sheer number of different approaches to your tasks, combined with the variety of the world, the items, the Vocations, and the ways they interact with each other, creates a unique experience for every Arisen.

You might even wonder why it says "Dragon's Dogma" at the beginning if this is the second game. Perhaps, by the end, you'll find your answer.

Everything in this world is intertwined. Vocations are connected to the world, and different skills can allow you to reach places you couldn't reach before. Vocations are connected to quests, quests are connected to other people, and your choices can lead to some really cool abilities and discoveries.

All of these systems come together to create a unique experience that, in my opinion, no other game can quite replicate.

And if you don't want to play DD2 because you've heard about its bad optimization, I have good news: the developers have done a great job improving it. The game now runs much more smoothly than it did at launch.

They also added another great quality-of-life feature: the Eternal Ferrystone, which lets you fast-travel as much as you want, so there's no more annoying backtracking.

That said, I still think DD2 could benefit from a proper hardcore mode.

[b]So overall, it's a 9/10 for me.[/b]

During my 2 hour’s gameplay I found this game to be nearly intolerable, let alone fun/enjoyable. This games only deserves 20USD price at best. 

• Combat tutorial is a huge mess. You’re stuffed with constant verbal instructions from NPC while focusing on the monster in front of you. I barely had time to try the first technique NPC taught me before them came up with the second technique. I even interrupted NPC’s combat instructions because I killed the monsters too quickly. As a sword&shield fighter playing normal difficulty, I just don’t have the that much energy to listen to what NPC was teaching me while defending myself from enemy blows. By the end of the combat I barely remember half of those combat tutorials.  

•The English dub was PAINFULLY plain and emotionless. I know people online praise this game of using medieval phrases but I feel like 2/3 of the NPCs were reading their script with no emotion at all. Even AI can do a better job than what’s in the game. There were no racism despises like Skyrim. There were no enthusiastic combat shouts like Helldiver. Everyone outside the cutscene sounds hollow. 

•The starting plot was horrible. I was very excited to gain freedom and starts to roam around the map but everything in my mouth turns bad the moment they introduced “pawns”. The player was brought up from the pitiful prisoner to a chosen champion where so many people would follow you blindly and for no reason all of a sudden. In any other games if you were to be given a companion, it would be a reason for either gold, friendship, life-saving but not in this game. It’s like using a cheat at the noob village but on the plot level which makes no sense and made me lost all the interest for the progression system. 
This is probably the worst thing in the game. “Pawns” are driving me nuts. I can’t imagine leading a group of mindless zombies with none of them being unique. I played Mass Effect and it was a shiny example of companionship. Each teammates have their own story and culture and personality. They interacts with each other and none of them is replaceable. I’d sacrifice millions of pawns in exchange for a one friendly NPC that isn’t a zombie manifested out of thin air. This is beyond stupid. 

I know I don’t have much time invested in this game. If it can’t hook me up in 2 hours, it’s not worth my time. I’d keep my game copy and support the dev if it’s cheap and has potential. But not in this case. This is an expensive slop made by a big company. So it’s not worth my money either.
